bibliographic.authors: Tzong-Gang Wu, Jung-Chi Chang, Sheng-Hsiu Huang, Wan-Yu Lin, Chang-Chuan Chan, Chang-Fu Wu (corresponding; National Taiwan University College of Public Health, Taipei)
bibliographic.title: Exposures and health impact for bicycle and electric scooter commuters in Taipei
bibliographic.journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment
bibliographic.volumeIssuePages: 91, article 102696 (10 pp. main text; page 11 has declarations)
bibliographic.funding: Department of Environmental Protection, Taipei City Government (Contract 106S060); Innovation and Policy Center for Population Health and Sustainable Environment (PHRC), NTU College of Public Health. No competing interests declared (p.11).
bibliographic.openAccess: unknown (no licence statement in the PDF)
bibliographic.citation: Wu T-G, Chang J-C, Huang S-H, Lin W-Y, Chan C-C, Wu C-F (2021). Exposures and health impact for bicycle and electric scooter commuters in Taipei. Transportation Research Part D 91:102696. doi:10.1016/j.trd.2021.102696

studyDesign: Mobile on-person monitoring along four roughly parallel downtown Taipei routes (A, B, C and reference route P; 3.58 to 5.29 km one way; enclosed area 17.2 km2), November 2017 to April 2018 (p.3). 82 runs (13 A, 12 B, 16 C, 41 P), each in forward and reverse direction, 40-80 min, on non-rainy days or RH under 80%, in two windows 08:30-10:30 (rush) and 13:30-15:30 (non-rush); pairs 'randomly assigned on weekdays'. A, B, C each paired with P, ridden by either bicycles (YouBike, 10-15 km/h) or ELECTRIC scooters (WeMo, 25-30 km/h) because of limited devices; riders were research assistants in pairs, not a sample of commuters; the scooters were electric 'to prevent self-pollution'. Route P had sidewalk bicycle lanes and 4+ lanes each way (LEZ demonstration by random inspection); A had a viaduct; B narrow with viaduct on half; C minor roads/alleys. BTEX: sorbent tube with active pump, inlet in breathing zone, thermal desorption GC-FID (US EPA TO-17), recovery-corrected (85.67-99.18%), integrated over each ride. PM2.5: DustTrak II 8530, 1 s, backpack, inlet in breathing zone, humidity-corrected (60-95% RH), data above 95% RH removed, calibrated to gravimetric. Body-worn camera video counted vehicles per minute (bus/truck, car, scooter, total). Analysis: GLMs for time-integrated values, mixed models for 1-min PM2.5, log-transformed, adjusted for best-correlated fixed-station measurement and wind; 1.5xIQR outliers removed. Ambient: four AQMS (PM2.5) and one PAMS (Wanhua) for BTEX. Health impact modelling after Tainio et al. 2016: relative risk of all-cause mortality from PM2.5 and benzene plus cycling physical-activity benefit versus staying home; durations 1.01 h (bicycle) and 0.79 h (scooter); backgrounds 13.46 ug/m3 PM2.5 and 2.54 ppb benzene (median x indoor/outdoor 0.70 and 0.90); 1000 lognormal draws. Sample sizes per mode/route/period, number of riders, and sampling height beyond 'breathing zone' are not given in the main text; supplementary material was not available to the checker.

findings.claim: The scooter commuters whose exposure was measured rode rented electric scooters, not gasoline scooters, so the study measured what a rider breathes from surrounding traffic, not a gasoline scooter's own tailpipe.
findings.value: n/a (design fact)
findings.quote: The use of an electric scooter instead of a gasoline-powered scooter prevented self-pollution during monitoring.
findings.caveats: Abstract and Table 1 label the group 'motorcyclists'/'scooter'. The paper never records the fuel type of other scooters in traffic; on p.9 the authors write of 'two-wheeled gasoline scooters' as an assumption about the traffic fleet, citing other work.
findings.useOnSite: The riders in this study used electric scooters on purpose, so the measured air reflects the surrounding traffic, not their own exhaust.
findings.checkerNote: Quote located (p.3, lines 147-148 of text). Whole 'scooter' group = WeMo/electric.

findings.claim: Average total BTEX and PM2.5 in the breathing zone were higher for electric-scooter commuters than cyclists in the printed means.
findings.value: Total BTEX 20.07 ppb (cyclists) vs 33.96 ppb (scooter commuters); PM2.5 23.27 ug/m3 vs 27.65 ug/m3
findings.quote: The average exposures of total BTEX and PM2.5 were 20.07 ppb and 23.27 ug/m3 for the cyclists and 33.96 ppb and 27.65 ug/m3 for the motorcyclists
findings.significance: No CI or test for these raw means. In the adjusted Table 1 model the bike-vs-scooter difference is significant for BTEX in rush hour and not significant for PM2.5.
findings.caveats: 'Motorcyclists' = electric scooter riders (p.3). Means pool routes, periods and an unstated number of runs; no SDs printed in text. UNRECONCILED: the dashed mean markers in Fig. 2 (p.4) read by eye at about 20 (bike) and about 28.5 (scooter) ppb total BTEX and about 22 and about 26.5 ug/m3 PM2.5, i.e. the scooter total BTEX and both PM2.5 marks sit below the printed values; the paper does not explain (outlier removal is a possible but unstated reason). Species means for scooters read from Fig. 2 sum to about 28.5, not 33.96.
findings.useOnSite: Riders in mixed Taipei traffic breathed on average about 34 ppb total BTEX and 28 ug/m3 PM2.5 (electric scooter riders, text values), versus 20 ppb and 23 ug/m3 for cyclists. Quote the printed figures and say the box-plot means look lower.
findings.checkerNote: Numbers confirmed against abstract and p.5. Added the Fig. 2 discrepancy found by opening p.4 at 300 dpi.

findings.claim: Mean exposure across the individual BTEX species and total BTEX spanned 2.59-20.07 ppb for cyclists and 4.02-33.96 ppb for scooter commuters; the text does not say which species is which.
findings.value: Cyclists 2.59 to 20.07 ppb; scooter commuters 4.02 to 33.96 ppb (range from lowest species to total BTEX)
findings.quote: Average BTEX exposure, including total BTEX, for bicycle commuters ranged between 2.59 and 20.07 ppb
findings.caveats: Reader's claim that benzene is the lowest species is NOT supported. Fig. 2 mean markers read by eye (ppb, bike/scooter): benzene about 2.6/4.2; toluene about 7.6/10.7; ethylbenzene about 2.6/3.5; m,p-xylene about 4.4/6.4; o-xylene about 2.8/3.8. For scooters ethylbenzene (about 3.5) and o-xylene (about 3.8) look lower than benzene, and none matches 4.02 exactly. Chart readings only; no per-species means are printed.
findings.useOnSite: Benzene was in the low single-digit ppb range for cyclists (about 2.6 ppb) and about 4 ppb for electric-scooter riders (Fig. 2 chart reading, not a printed value); similar in size to ethylbenzene and o-xylene.
findings.checkerNote: Removed 'benzene lowest species' and the 'benzene median 2.5/4 ppb' framing; benzene medians read about 2.5 and 3.9, means about 2.6 and 4.2.

findings.claim: The main text does not tabulate benzene or other single species as numbers by group or route; only Fig. 2 (modes pooled over routes/periods) and Table 1 (percent differences) carry species-level results. Per-route descriptives are in supplementary Table S2.
findings.value: n/a
findings.quote: General descriptive statistics for the routes are provided in Table S2.
findings.caveats: Supplement (Tables S1, S2, HIM details) not available to the checker.
findings.useOnSite: Per-route benzene and PM2.5 means must come from the supplement (Table S2); the main text gives only percent differences by route.
findings.checkerNote: Confirmed; page of the Table S2 sentence is 7.

findings.claim: Cyclists' BTEX was higher than reported for North American and European cities; scooter commuters' BTEX and PM2.5 were much lower than in Taipei studies 10-20 years earlier. Comparison values are in supplementary Table S1.
findings.value: Qualitative; no numbers in main text
findings.quote: exposures are relatively higher in Taipei and other Asian cities than in European and North American cities
findings.caveats: The comparison with North America/Europe is stated for cyclists' BTEX and PM2.5; for scooter commuters the comparison is with Taipei 20 years ago (BTEX, Chan 1994) and Vietnam (Lan 2013), and PM2.5 with 'some cities, including Taipei City, 10 years ago'. Authors read the fall as 'an improvement in the transportation environment'.
findings.useOnSite: Exposure in this study was lower than in older Taipei studies, so the paper's numbers are not a worst case; the paper gives no number for the comparison in the main text.
findings.checkerNote: Specified which group each comparison refers to.

findings.claim: The paper reports correlations between on-road and fixed-station data but no ambient concentration values to compare against; on-road PM2.5 tracked ambient closely while BTEX did not.
findings.value: PM2.5 r = 0.67 to 0.86; BTEX r = -0.01 to 0.38 (both periods)
findings.locator: Section 3.2 (text runs over p.5 to p.7)
findings.quote: The correlation coefficients ranged from -0.01 to 0.38 in both periods
findings.caveats: Ambient BTEX came from one PAMS (Wanhua AQMS); PM2.5 from four AQMS. Authors: 'using ambient measurements to assess commuter exposure to BTEXs might result in biased results.' Paper cannot say how much higher street-level benzene is than ambient.
findings.useOnSite: Fixed-station BTEX readings did not track on-road BTEX (r up to 0.38), so street-level benzene cannot be inferred from monitoring stations.
findings.checkerNote: Page fixed: the r values are on p.7, not p.6.

findings.claim: On the same days, all pollutants were significantly higher in rush hour than non-rush hour.
findings.value: Mean rush/non-rush ratios 1.26 to 1.87 (26 same-day pairs); lowest lower 95% CI bound 1.01 (PM2.5)
findings.quote: The mean ratios ranged between 1.26 and 1.87 for the BTEXs and PM2.5 ... All exposures were significantly higher during the rush hour period (P < 0.05).
findings.significance: P < 0.05 for all; PM2.5 CI lower bound about 1.0. Chart readings: benzene mean about 1.87 (CI about 1.2 to 2.55); total BTEX about 1.6 (CI about 1.1 to 2.1); PM2.5 about 1.26 (CI about 1.0 to 1.5).
findings.caveats: 26 pairs; riding modes pooled. Ratios of rush to non-rush exposure, not concentration differences.
findings.useOnSite: Benzene exposure was on average about 1.9 times higher in the morning rush than in the afternoon on the same days (chart reading, 95% CI about 1.2 to 2.6); PM2.5 about 1.3 times.
findings.checkerNote: Page corrected to 7 (Section 3.3 is on p.7; figure on p.5). Added total BTEX reading.

findings.claim: The minor-road route C gave significantly lower exposure than the main reference route P in rush hour for total BTEX, benzene and PM2.5 (not toluene).
findings.value: Rush hour, Route C vs P: total BTEX -24.27% (*), benzene -33.20% (*), toluene -14.31% (n.s., P = 0.35), ethylbenzene -21.34% (*), m,p-xylene -29.32% (*), o-xylene -28.89% (*), PM2.5 -27.7% (*), 1-min PM2.5 -28.10% (**)
findings.locator: Table 1, rush hour, Route C; Section 3.4
findings.significance: * P<0.05, ** P<0.001. Non-rush Route C: total BTEX -10.06% n.s., benzene -4.63% n.s., PM2.5 -18.4% n.s. (GLM) but 1-min PM2.5 -21.75% (**), ethylbenzene -11.73% (*), o-xylene -15.19% (*).
findings.caveats: Percent changes from log-transformed models adjusted for ambient levels and wind with mode as covariate; reference = Route P. Route C had lowest traffic (about 9 vehicles/min rush, Fig. 4) and about 30 signals vs 38 on P. Route C is minor roads/alleys in residential and business areas.
findings.useOnSite: A quieter side-street route had about a third less benzene and about 28% less PM2.5 than the main road in rush hour, adjusted for ambient and wind.
findings.checkerNote: All cells checked on the Table 1 image (p.6). Non-rush PM2.5 text says it stayed different; the GLM cell has no star, the 1-min cell does.

findings.claim: Routes A and B, with a viaduct and (for B) narrow street canyons, were not lower than route P despite less traffic; Route B was significantly higher for ethylbenzene and 1-min PM2.5 in rush hour, and for 1-min PM2.5 in non-rush hour too.
findings.value: Route B rush hour: ethylbenzene +22.73% (*), 1-min PM2.5 +10.69% (*); Route B non-rush: 1-min PM2.5 +6.19% (*); Route A: no significant differences. Aspect ratios H/W A 0.87 (0.47), B 1.54 (1.09), C 1.20 (0.78), P 0.69 (0.21)
findings.quote: the street canyon of Route B played a substantial role in increasing the exposures
findings.caveats: Canyon explanation is the authors' interpretation, not tested directly. Route-average PM2.5 on B (+33.0%, rush) was not significant. Route B has about 14 vehicles/min vs 24 on P (Fig. 4, chart reading).
findings.useOnSite: Street geometry matters as well as traffic: the narrowest, enclosed route had higher ethylbenzene and 1-minute PM2.5 than the main road despite less traffic (authors' interpretation).
findings.checkerNote: Added the non-rush Route B 1-min PM2.5 +6.19% (*) cell the reader missed; pages extended.

findings.claim: Cyclists had significantly lower BTEX exposure than electric-scooter riders in rush hour, but PM2.5 did not differ significantly. The authors attribute the gap to where riders can wait and ride; this was not tested.
findings.significance: * P<0.05, ** P<0.001. PM2.5 not significant in either period.
findings.caveats: Comparison is bicycle vs ELECTRIC scooter, not gasoline. Authors: 'bicycle commuters can choose the place (e.g., on the sidewalk) to wait for a traffic light or ride on bicycle lanes, scooter commuters can only ride on the road with motor vehicles, which enclose them in emissions.' Not tested; bikes and scooters also differ in speed (10-15 vs 25-30 km/h) and mode was not randomised within routes. Route P had dedicated bicycle lanes on sidewalks (p.3). Subjects were research assistants, not pedestrians.
findings.useOnSite: Cyclists (10-15 km/h, bike lanes and sidewalks available) breathed about 40% less benzene in rush hour than electric-scooter riders on the same routes (adjusted model); the authors attribute it to riding on the road among motor vehicles. The paper did not measure people standing at lights, and PM2.5 differences were not significant.
findings.checkerNote: Reader's wording 'people waiting at lights on the sidewalk ... breathed about 40% less' overstated: nobody was measured waiting; riders were measured en route. Added PM2.5 non-rush cells.

findings.claim: The authors infer PM2.5 varied less between places and modes than BTEX, linked to PM2.5 being more regionally mixed and partly secondary.
findings.value: n/a
findings.quote: BTEXs had higher spatial variation than did PM2.5
findings.caveats: Inference from low BTEX-ambient correlation and non-significant PM2.5 mode difference; not tested separately. The reader's extension 'benzene is the better marker of local traffic exhaust' is not stated by the authors; the paper says BTEX has higher spatial variation and that ambient stations may mis-estimate commuter BTEX.
findings.useOnSite: Benzene and other BTEX varied more from street to street than PM2.5 did (authors' inference).
findings.checkerNote: Pages 7 and 8 (not 6); removed the 'better marker of traffic exhaust' claim, which is the reader's inference.

findings.claim: Traffic volume and number of traffic signals differed by route; the authors cite stop-and-go driving as raising pollutants but did not measure idling or queues.
findings.value: Signals: A 46, B 46, C about 30, P 38. Mean vehicles/min (Fig. 4, chart readings): rush A about 10, B about 14, C about 9, P about 24; non-rush A about 15.5, B about 11.5, C about 8, P about 17
findings.quote: A high frequency of stop-and-go driving behavior in the traffic fleet can cause higher concentrations of pollutants such as PM2.5 and UFP (Zwack et al., 2011).
findings.caveats: The stop-and-go statement is a citation, not a result. Fig. 4 values are chart readings (all four checked on the image). Route A had more traffic in non-rush than rush hour.
findings.useOnSite: The paper counted traffic lights per route (30 to 46) and cites stop-and-go as raising pollution, but did not measure pollution at red lights.
findings.checkerNote: Signals and chart values checked.

findings.claim: Per additional vehicle passing each minute, buses/trucks raised on-road 1-min PM2.5 about 8 to 10 times more than scooters; the scooter increment exceeded the passenger-car increment.
findings.value: Separate models: +0.41 (bus/truck), +0.04 (car), +0.05 (scooter) ug/m3 per vehicle/min. Joint model: +0.29, +0.01, +0.03 ug/m3
findings.quote: each additional bus/truck, passenger car, and scooter increased the one-minute PM2.5 exposure by 0.41, 0.04, and 0.05 ug/m3, respectively
findings.caveats: Authors cite other work (not measured here) that diesel buses/trucks have the highest PM2.5 emission rate and 'two-wheeled gasoline scooters have the lowest'; yet their own coefficients put scooters above passenger cars (0.05 vs 0.04 separate; 0.03 vs 0.01 joint). Authors' proximity explanation is untested. 'Scooter' in the count is not split by fuel. Mixed model includes ambient PM2.5 and wind. Rider's own vehicle (bicycle or electric scooter) is not stated to be excluded from counts.
findings.useOnSite: One passing bus or truck added far more PM2.5 than one scooter (0.29 vs 0.03 ug/m3 per vehicle/min, joint model); scooters matter because there are so many.
findings.checkerNote: Page was 8-9; numbers are on p.9. Clarified scooter vs car ordering; see complication fix.

findings.claim: Because scooters were the most numerous vehicle, they made the largest modelled contribution to riders' 1-min PM2.5, but the absolute increments were small.
findings.value: Mean vehicles per minute (SD): bus/truck 0.35 (1.14), car 7.2 (8.49), scooter 8.56 (9.29). Modelled contribution: 0.10 ug/m3 (bus/truck), 0.10 (car), 0.28 (scooter)
findings.quote: The average exposure concentrations were 0.10, 0.10, and 0.28 ug/m3 for buses/trucks, passenger cars, and scooters, respectively.
findings.caveats: Paper says only 'model coefficients ... multiplied by the average traffic count'. The printed contributions match the unrounded joint-model coefficients (0.29 x 0.35 = 0.10); the separate-model coefficients would give about 0.14, 0.29, 0.43, so the joint model is the likely basis (inference). Checker arithmetic: sum 0.48 ug/m3, scooters about 58% (not stated in paper); scooter 0.28 is about 1% of the 27.65 ug/m3 mean, but the paper does not partition the rest, so 'most PM2.5 is from other sources' is an inference. Authors: 'Although the magnitude of these exposure increments seems to be small, cumulative doses can be substantial after considering commuting time.' Counted scooters not stated to be gasoline.
findings.useOnSite: Of the PM2.5 added by the traffic types in the model, scooters accounted for the largest share (0.28 of about 0.48 ug/m3, checker arithmetic), because there were about 9 per minute against 0.35 buses/trucks.
findings.checkerNote: Page 9 confirmed. Added basis-of-calculation note and flagged the 1% / background statement as inference.

findings.claim: The authors explain the bike advantage by where cyclists wait at signals versus where scooter riders ride.
findings.value: n/a
findings.quote: scooter commuters can only ride on the road with motor vehicles, which enclose them in emissions
findings.caveats: Explanation offered, not tested with at-signal data. Same sentence as the bike-vs-scooter finding.
findings.useOnSite: The authors attribute the higher exposure of road users to being enclosed among motor vehicles at lights and in traffic.
findings.checkerNote: Quote on p.8, lines 391-392.

findings.claim: The authors suggest scooters' contribution exceeds cars' per vehicle because riders keep closer to scooters and bicycles than to buses, trucks and cars.
findings.value: n/a
findings.quote: scooter and bicycle commuters being close, owing to the behavior of the riders in Taiwan tending to maintain a safe distance from buses, trucks, and passenger cars
findings.caveats: Hypothesis; proximity not measured. Concerns riders sharing the road, not pedestrians.
findings.useOnSite: Proximity to the source is the authors' stated possible reason scooters weigh heavily in exposure.
findings.checkerNote: Quote located p.9.

findings.claim: With PM2.5 alone and the physical-activity benefit included, cyclists come out below break-even (benefit) while scooter commuters sit at about 1.0 (no benefit, no extra harm).
findings.value: Scenario A, PM2.5 only, median (10th-90th): bike rush 0.85 (0.84-0.87), bike non-rush 0.84 (0.83-0.85), scooter rush 1.00 (1.00-1.02), scooter non-rush 1.00 (1.00-1.03)
findings.quote: Bike Rush hour 0.85 0.84 0.87; Scooter Rush hour 1.00 1.00 1.02
findings.significance: Interval = 10th-90th percentile of 1000 lognormal draws of exposure inputs only. Unitless; 1 = break-even versus staying home; below 1 = benefit.
findings.caveats: Long-term all-cause mortality relative-risk measure for an individual adult commuter, assuming the measured exposure and 1.01 h (bike) / 0.79 h (scooter) per day persist. Scooter riders get no physical-activity credit. Not an observed outcome. Applies to riders, not pedestrians.
findings.useOnSite: For PM2.5 alone, cycling's activity benefit outweighed its pollution risk in this model; electric-scooter riding showed neither benefit nor harm (1.00).
findings.checkerNote: Table 2 checked on the page image.

findings.claim: Adding benzene pushed central estimates above break-even for both modes in Scenario A, which the authors read as single-pollutant models underestimating harm.
findings.value: Scenario A, benzene + PM2.5, median (10th-90th): bike rush 1.18 (0.91-2.98), bike non-rush 1.05 (0.89-2.13), scooter rush 1.25 (1.09-1.72), scooter non-rush 1.05 (1.00-115.72)
findings.quote: the central HIM estimates for both commuters were greater than the breakeven point (one) in all given conditions for Scenario A. This indicates that HIM can underestimate health impact when based on a single-pollutant assessment.
findings.significance: Intervals very wide; bike rush interval includes values below 1 (0.91); bike non-rush lower bound 0.89.
findings.caveats: Benzene dose-response is a single Toronto cohort (Villeneuve 2013, nonaccidental mortality), cited p.2; details in the supplement. On p.10 the authors say the extreme 90th-percentile values in non-rush periods 'were the repeated sampling results from the lognormal distributions' (said of Scenario B; the 115.72 in Scenario A non-rush is of the same kind). Background 13.46 ug/m3 PM2.5 and 2.54 ppb benzene is the study's own median times indoor/outdoor ratios 0.70 and 0.90 (p.5, 9), not measured ambient. Scenario B non-rush bike medians (0.88, 0.90) are below 1 while Scenario A non-rush bike is 1.05; the paper does not reconcile these.
findings.useOnSite: When benzene is included, the model's central estimate for rush-hour electric-scooter riders is 1.25 (10th-90th 1.09-1.72), but the intervals are wide and the benzene effect rests on one cohort study.
findings.checkerNote: Replaced 'artefacts' (reader's word) with the authors' wording and scope; added Scenario A vs B non-rush bike inconsistency.

findings.claim: In Scenario B (routes C vs P), rush-hour estimates were lower on quiet route C for both modes; electric-scooter commuters were above break-even on all routes and periods when benzene was included.
findings.value: Benzene+PM2.5 median (10th-90th): bike C rush 1.02 (0.96-1.11), bike C non-rush 0.88 (0.84-16.67), bike P rush 1.12 (1.02-1.28), bike P non-rush 0.90 (0.84-26.28), scooter C rush 1.17 (1.09-1.33), scooter C non-rush 1.05 (1.01-2.5), scooter P rush 1.25 (1.13-1.53), scooter P non-rush 1.06 (1.01-2.98). PM2.5 only: bikes 0.84 in all four; scooters 1.00-1.01
findings.quote: the HIM estimates for the scooter commuters were always greater than the breakeven point due to the lack of PA
findings.significance: Same 10th-90th percentile uncertainty; Route C inputs synthesised as Route P data times Table 1 percent changes (p.9).
findings.caveats: Scooter excess is attributed by the authors to lack of physical activity, so it reflects missing benefit plus benzene, not only pollution. Riders modelled are electric scooter riders.
findings.useOnSite: Choosing the quiet street lowered the modelled rush-hour estimate from 1.25 to 1.17 for scooter riders and from 1.12 to 1.02 for cyclists.
findings.checkerNote: All 16 cells verified against Table 2.

findings.claim: The authors estimate how long a bike commute can last before benzene plus PM2.5 offsets the activity benefit.
findings.value: Rush hour: under about 0.4 h on Route P, under about 0.8 h on Route C; non-rush: acceptable for under 2 h on both routes
findings.quote: In the rush hour period, travel time should be approximately less than 0.4 h on Route P and less than 0.8 h on Route C.
findings.caveats: Fig. 5 curves cross 1.0 at about 0.4 h (P) and about 0.85 h (C), matching the text. Shows pollution can cancel the exercise benefit for cyclists in heavy rush-hour traffic. Concerns adult cyclists, not pedestrians.
findings.useOnSite: In heavy rush-hour traffic the model says the pollution cost cancels cycling's benefit after about 24 minutes on a main road, but not until about 48 minutes on a quiet one.
findings.checkerNote: Fig. 5 checked.

findings.claim: The authors conclude that gasoline-powered scooter commuters should be reduced and commuters moved to bicycles.
findings.value: n/a
findings.quote: Reducing the number of gasoline-powered scooter commuters may help reduce exposure.
findings.caveats: No gasoline scooter was measured; conclusion rests on the traffic-count regression and cited emission literature. Abstract: 'the number of scooters in traffic should be reduced, and commuters should be encouraged to shift from gasoline scooters to bicycles'.
findings.useOnSite: The authors recommend fewer gasoline scooters in traffic, but this is their conclusion from traffic-count associations, not a measured gasoline-scooter result.
findings.checkerNote: Quotes located.

findings.claim: The authors call shifting commuters from scooters to bicycles or public transport an urgent policy priority.
findings.value: n/a
findings.quote: For policymakers, encouraging people to change their commuting mode from scooter to bicycle or public transportation to reduce urban air pollution must be an urgent priority.
findings.caveats: This sentence does not name electric scooters; p.9 lists 'public transportation (including electric scooter systems), or personal electric scooters' among options that 'can result in improved outcomes'.
findings.useOnSite: The paper's policy call is mode shift to bicycles or public transport; electric scooters appear as an acceptable option in the discussion.
findings.checkerNote: Quote located.

findings.claim: The paper names electric scooters (shared or personal) as one way to cut the number of gasoline scooters, with no estimate of benefit.
findings.value: No numerical benefit estimate
findings.quote: reducing the number of gasoline scooters by shifting to commuting by bicycle, public transportation (including electric scooter systems), or personal electric scooters can result in improved outcomes
findings.caveats: Not quantified or modelled; no electric-vs-gasoline comparison. Riders in the study were on electric scooters and still had higher BTEX than cyclists because of surrounding traffic.
findings.useOnSite: The authors list electric scooters among shifts that would help, without quantifying it.
findings.checkerNote: Quote located p.9.

findings.claim: Route P had a low emission zone demonstration but the largest traffic volume; it was the reference route.
findings.value: Route P about 24 vehicles/min in rush hour (Fig. 4); 38 signals
findings.quote: Route P has an LEZ policy (implemented as an initial demonstration) and a relatively open street canyon geometry, but it had the largest traffic volume among the routes
findings.caveats: LEZ was enforced by random spot inspections of entering vehicles (p.3), so it is not a test of the policy. Reader's claim that P had 'the highest exposures among the routes' is not supported: Table 1 shows Routes A and B with higher (non-significant) values in places; the paper says only that P's pollutants were higher than C's.
findings.useOnSite: The only low-emission-zone route studied was a spot-check demonstration, so the paper says nothing on whether an LEZ works.
findings.checkerNote: Page 3 (not 2) for Section 2.1; dropped 'highest exposures'.

limitations: Authors (p.10): BTEX time-integrated over whole rides, so short-term variation (e.g. at red lights) could not be evaluated.
Authors (p.10): relatively small sample size limits representativeness; uncertainty analysis only partly addresses it.
Authors (p.10): seasonality could not be assessed (Nov 2017 to Apr 2018 only).
Group sample sizes by mode, route and period are not in the main text (only 82 runs, 13/12/16/41 by route).
Mode not randomised within routes; each paired run was bicycle OR electric scooter depending on available devices; riders were research assistants at prescribed speeds.
HIM background is the study's own medians times assumed indoor/outdoor ratios, not measured ambient; counterfactual is staying home; long-term persistence of exposure assumed.
Benzene dose-response from a single Toronto cohort (nonaccidental mortality); intervals up to 115.72.
Fig. 2 mean markers do not match some printed means (scooter total BTEX, PM2.5).
complications: The scooter commuters measured rode ELECTRIC scooters. No gasoline scooter rider was measured and no gasoline-vs-electric comparison exists; exposure came from surrounding traffic.
PM2.5 did not differ significantly between bike and electric-scooter riders (P = 0.07 rush, 0.97 non-rush; 1-min P = 0.14, 0.86); only BTEX did.

Per vehicle, scooters added far less PM2.5 than buses/trucks (0.03-0.05 vs 0.29-0.41 ug/m3); the authors cite scooters as having the lowest emission rate, although their own coefficients put scooters above cars (0.05 vs 0.04; 0.03 vs 0.01). The scooter contribution (0.28 ug/m3) is about 1% of the 23-28 ug/m3 mean.
'Scooter' in the traffic-count regression is not split by fuel type, and the regression covers PM2.5 only; benzene could not be attributed to vehicle types.
Exposures were much lower than in earlier Taipei studies (BTEX 20 years earlier, PM2.5 10 years earlier).

The strongest 'harm' result (HIM above 1 with benzene) is partly because scooter riders get no physical-activity credit and rests on one benzene cohort with intervals up to 115.72; with PM2.5 alone scooters are 1.00-1.01.
Cyclists with benzene included had rush-hour medians above 1 on Route P (1.12) and in Scenario A (1.18); the model does not show cycling to be harmless in main-road rush-hour traffic.
The bike advantage is a rider-behaviour comparison, untested at signals; bikes are slower (10-15 vs 25-30 km/h) and had sidewalk bike lanes on Route P.
The paper recommends mode shift to bicycles or public transport and has no estimate of the benefit of replacing gasoline with electric scooters.
Nothing was measured on pedestrians, children, older people or roadside workers; all subjects were adult research-assistant riders.
No intersection, red-light or idling measurements; stop-and-go is only cited from other work.
Street canyon geometry and traffic both mattered (Route B higher than P despite less traffic), so traffic volume alone does not explain exposure.
correctionsToAbstractLevelNotes: Abstract 'motorcyclists' and 'scooter' commuters rode rented electric scooters (p.3), not gasoline scooters.

Abstract 'Scooters could contribute more to PM2.5 exposure than buses/trucks and passenger cars' is because of count (8.56/min vs 0.35 buses/trucks); per vehicle buses/trucks contribute about 8-10 times more; contributions 0.28 vs 0.10 vs 0.10 ug/m3, small against about 25 ug/m3.

Abstract means (20.07 vs 33.96 ppb; 23.27 vs 27.65 ug/m3) are unadjusted; in the adjusted model only BTEX differs significantly, not PM2.5; Fig. 2 mean markers look lower than the printed scooter means.
Abstract's call to shift 'from gasoline scooters to bicycles' is a recommendation resting on the traffic-count regression and cited emissions work, not on measurements of gasoline scooters.
The paper gives no per-species means in text and no ambient concentration values; BTEX correlation with the ambient station was r up to 0.38.
The health impact is a modelled all-cause mortality relative-risk for an individual adult commuter, not an observed outcome, and the scooter excess is largely the missing physical-activity benefit.

answersToQuestions: 1. Electric. Scooter measurements used electric scooters rented from WeMo: 'The use of an electric scooter instead of a gasoline-powered scooter prevented self-pollution during monitoring' (p.3). The abstract's 'motorcyclists' and Table 1's 'scooter' group are these electric-scooter riders. The title's 'electric scooter' is the riders' vehicle (measurement platform); the pollution came from surrounding traffic, whose fuel mix is not recorded. The authors still frame conclusions around reducing 'gasoline-powered scooter' commuters.

2. Four routes (A, B, C, reference P; 3.58-5.29 km one way) in downtown Taipei, Nov 2017 to Apr 2018; 82 runs (13 A, 12 B, 16 C, 41 P), forward and reverse, 40-80 min; 08:30-10:30 and 13:30-15:30; weekdays, non-rainy or RH<80%. Research-assistant riders in pairs on YouBike bicycles (10-15 km/h) or WeMo electric scooters (25-30 km/h). BTEX by sorbent tube, active pump, thermal desorption GC-FID (EPA TO-17), integrated over the ride; PM2.5 by DustTrak II 8530 at 1 s in a backpack; both inlets 'in the breathing zone' (no numeric height). Camera video for traffic counts; four AQMS and one PAMS for ambient. Subjects were the assistants, not a population sample; number of riders and per-group samples not stated.

3. Printed means: total BTEX 20.07 (bike) vs 33.96 ppb (scooter); PM2.5 23.27 vs 27.65 ug/m3; species-and-total means ranged 2.59-20.07 (bike) and 4.02-33.96 ppb (scooter), not labelled by species. Fig. 2 chart readings (ppb, bike/scooter): benzene about 2.6/4.2, toluene about 7.6/10.7, ethylbenzene about 2.6/3.5, m,p-xylene about 4.4/6.4, o-xylene about 2.8/3.8; benzene is not clearly the lowest. m,p-xylene is about 22% of total BTEX. SDs/ranges only as Fig. 2 percentiles and supplement. By route (Table 1, % vs Route P, adjusted): rush Route C total BTEX -24.27%, benzene -33.20%, PM2.5 -27.7%; Route B ethylbenzene +22.73%, 1-min PM2.5 +10.69%; Route A none significant. Absolute route means are in Table S2 (not seen). No ambient concentrations are reported; correlations with stations PM2.5 r 0.67-0.86, BTEX r -0.01 to 0.38. Compared with other cities (Table S1): cyclists' BTEX higher than North America/Europe; scooter-commuter values lower than Taipei 10-20 years earlier.

4. Mixed regression of 1-min PM2.5 on video-counted vehicles per minute, controlling for ambient PM2.5 and wind (BTEX not used because time-integrated). Per vehicle/min: separate models 0.41 (bus/truck), 0.04 (car), 0.05 (scooter) ug/m3; joint 0.29, 0.01, 0.03. Mean counts/min 0.35, 7.2, 8.56. Contribution 0.10, 0.10, 0.28 ug/m3 (p.9), so scooters 'made the greatest contribution' through numbers. Scooter fuel not distinguished; no CIs printed.

5. Health impact modelling after Tainio et al. 2016: change in relative risk of all-cause mortality from PM2.5 (and benzene in the second variant, one Toronto cohort function) plus cycling physical-activity benefit, versus staying home; inputs measured exposures, durations 1.01 h/0.79 h, backgrounds 13.46 ug/m3 and 2.54 ppb, 1000 lognormal draws. Table 2 medians (1 = break-even): PM2.5 only bike 0.84-0.85, scooter 1.00-1.01; with benzene Scenario A bike 1.18 rush/1.05 non-rush, scooter 1.25/1.05; Scenario B scooter P rush 1.25, C rush 1.17, bike P rush 1.12, C rush 1.02, bike non-rush 0.88-0.90. 10th-90th ranges wide (up to 115.72). Applies to adult riders; not pedestrians or children.

6. 'Reducing the number of gasoline-powered scooter commuters may help reduce exposure.' (p.10); 'riding a scooter (without the beneficial effects of PA) was still harmful to health.' (p.10); 'Riding a bicycle may result in a higher dose of pollutants, but choosing proper routes, periods, and commuting duration can improve potential health status.' (p.10); 'For policymakers, encouraging people to change their commuting mode from scooter to bicycle or public transportation to reduce urban air pollution must be an urgent priority.' (p.10); 'Commuting by bicycle also led to lower exposure to BTEXs than did commuting by electric scooters.' (p.10). Abstract: 'the number of scooters in traffic should be reduced, and commuters should be encouraged to shift from gasoline scooters to bicycles'. Electric scooters: p.9 lists 'public transportation (including electric scooter systems), or personal electric scooters' as shifts that 'can result in improved outcomes'.

7. Little and indirect. No measurement at intersections, red lights or idling; BTEX integrated over whole rides so red-light effects could not be examined (p.10). Signals counted per route (A 46, B 46, C about 30, P 38) and stop-and-go cited from Zwack 2011 to explain low Route C (p.8). Authors say cyclists can wait on the sidewalk or use bike lanes whereas scooter riders 'can only ride on the road with motor vehicles, which enclose them in emissions' (p.8), untested. Rush-hour ratio 1.26-1.87 (p.7).

8. No. No estimate of benefit from replacing gasoline with electric scooters and no electric-vs-gasoline emission or exposure comparison; only the qualitative statement on p.9. Quantified comparisons are bicycle vs electric scooter and Route C vs P.
